query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high‐entropy alloys for fusion plasma‐facing components, the high‐temperature plastic strain and toughness are primarily governed by the degree of lattice distortion that modifies the core structure of mobile edge dislocations. Increased lattice distortion forces the dislocation cores to adopt a wavy configuration, which impedes their glide and enhances strain hardening, ultimately delaying plastic instability and improving toughness at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a BCC solid solution similar to NbTaTiV) exhibiting a baseline level of lattice distortion due to compositional fluctuations from differing atomic radii.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by substituting one or more elements with either larger or more similar atomic radii to respectively increase or decrease the lattice distortion, while keeping phase stability, grain size, and processing routes constant.
generation.conditions: High‐temperature mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or compressive tests) performed at temperatures relevant to fusion plasma conditions (600–900°C) under controlled strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion-induced modification of dislocation core geometry (specifically, the transition of <111>{110} edge dislocation cores from a straight to a wavy configuration).
generation.mechanism: The heterogeneity in atomic sizes within the alloy produces severe local lattice distortions. These distortions force edge dislocation cores to deviate from their neutral planes, creating wavy dislocation lines that slow down dislocation glide. This retardation increases the capacity for strain hardening and delays the initiation of catastrophic failure, thereby enhancing the material’s toughness even at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy variants engineered to have a higher degree of lattice distortion will display (a) increased evidence of wavy dislocation cores through in situ microstructural characterization, and (b) improved high-temperature strain hardening and toughness compared to baseline alloys with lower lattice distortion, despite possibly lower yield strengths.
generation.baseline: The original alloy composition with its inherent level of lattice distortion and associated high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in single-phase, BCC refractory high-entropy alloys under high-temperature (600–900°C) deformation conditions with controlled strain rates. It may not apply to multi-phase alloys or systems where other mechanisms (such as screw dislocation dominated plasticity) prevail.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitatively relating the degree of lattice distortion to the balance between strength and toughness remains uncertain, and other microstructural factors (grain boundary effects, residual stresses) may also influence the observed high-temperature behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of BCC refractory high-entropy alloys: one with increased lattice distortion (via intentional elemental substitutions to enhance atomic radii mismatch) and one with reduced lattice distortion (via choosing elements with more similar atomic sizes). Process both sets under identical conditions and perform high-temperature mechanical tests (600–900°C) under controlled strain rates. Use in-situ techniques such as neutron diffraction and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess the dislocation core configurations.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength and fracture strength
Plastic strain to failure and strain hardening rate
Quantitative characterization of dislocation core morphology (e.g., degree of waviness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with increased lattice distortion does not show a statistically significant increase in strain hardening and toughness, nor display more pronounced wavy dislocation cores compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness is falsified.

System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99 wt% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling.
